fig1_model: How a model feeding encounter works. (a) Dolphins maintain near-prey pressure for a minimum duration, pursue a feasible target and recover. Their rules do not change with bird presence. (b,c) Top and side views of one recorded encounter at 12 model-time units, with paths and captures from 6–12. This illustrates geometry, not proof of a compact bait ball.
fig2_returns: Absolute feeding returns and matched partner benefits through eighteen gannets. (a,b) Captures per dolphin or gannet over the complete 36T encounter; dashed lines show matched single-species controls. Bird-only controls at each count are shared across H. (c,d) Changes relative to those controls: faint points show four paired school effects; bands and bars are exploratory pointwise 95% intervals for their means. Actual numeric bird-count spacing is retained.
fig3_opportunities: Herding duration changes strike opportunities and prey state. (a) Launches per dolphin; (b) eligible contacts per launch; (c) eligible contacts per dolphin; (d) live-fish r90. Counts cover 36T, including bird-free controls. Faint points show schools; lines join equal-school means except (b), which pools contacts/launches. r90 uses trapezoidal time averages over nonempty frames. School-state changes do not by themselves establish a feeding mechanism.
fig4_sensitivity: Selected mutual benefits and separate numerical sensitivity. (a,b) Four-school dolphin and bird effects at H = 1T with nine birds and H = 2T with twelve birds, using matched controls and pointwise 95% intervals. (c,d) The distinct eight-school H = 2T, three-bird check across original and halved timesteps; only original means have 97.5% marginal intervals. Axes show changes per individual predator over 36T: twelve dolphins throughout, nine/twelve birds above and three below. Thin lines connect the same school, diamonds mark means, and bars show the stated intervals. Schools and settings must not be pooled.
